subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Of course, Mr. Speaker, I accept your ruling. With no thought of referring to any previous debate of this session, I merely wished to comment briefly on a section of the British North America Act. It is section 133, which reads as follows:
Either the English or the French language may be used by any person in the debates of the houses of parliament of Canada and of the houses of the legislature of Quebec; and both those languages shall be used in the respective records and journals of those houses; and either of those languages may be used by any person or in any pleading or process in or issuing from any court of Canada established under this Act. and in or from all or any of the courts of Quebec.
The Acts of the parliament of Canada and of the legislature of Quebec shall be printed and published in both those languages.
I maintain, Mr. Speaker, that even those who hold the view that the constitution may be amended without consulting the provinces must admit-and I except no one-that there are sections of the British North America Act which cannot be modified without the previous consent of one or several of the provinces whenever such province or provinces are directly concerned by the provision whose modification is contemplated. Now section 133 specially and directly concerns the province of Quebec. It deals with the debates in the legislature of Quebec and with proceedings in the courts of that province. The claim that this house could amend this section would mean that the dominion parliament could compel members of the Quebec legislature to carry on their debates in the English language. The mere thought of it is so extraordinary that it verges on the absurd. Now, I have never seen any absurdity sanctioned by law and this argument is very often set forth in all courts of justice.
Mr. Speaker, there have been occasions, since 1760, where the French Canadian have had to complain of the treatment meted out to them in this country. In references to the settlement of past problems, the impression is often conveyed that all difficulties were adjusted through the magnanimity of the masters of the time.
If controversies arising out of the language and the rights of French Canadians were solved in former days it is mostly because French-Canadian representatives, either in the Union Parliament which lasted from 1840 to 1867 or afterwards insisted upon and demanded the recognition of our rights. I recall no chapter in history more inspiring than that which relates the 1842 session of the Union Parliament, when Louis Hippolyte Lafontaine took his seat as a member. The events to which I have just referred are narrated in page 36 of Hon. L. 0. David's book "LTJnion des deux Canadas." As I said a moment ago, these happenings occurred in 1842, and the excerpt reads as follows:
When the Hon. Denis Benjamin Viger had concluded his eloquent speech, Mr. Lafontaine took the floor.
A tremor of curiosity passed through the house and galleries as Mr. Lafontaine rose; people wished to see and hear the man whose name, for some time past, carried so much weight. For many, however, curiosity gave way to surprise and disappointment when" he addressed himself to the chairman of the house in French. Mr. Dunn having asked him to speak in English, he answered:
"Has the hon. member forgotten that I belong to the nationality which was the object of such unfair discrimination by the Act of Union? He asks me to use for my maiden speech in this house a language other than my mother tongue. I am diffident about my ability to express myself in the English language, but even if I spoke it as fluently as an Englishman. I would nonetheless make my first speech in the tongue of my French-Canadian fellow-countrymen, were it only to protest solemnly against the cruel injustice perpetuated in that part of the Act of Union which tends to outlaw the mother tongue of half of Canada's population. This much I owe to my fellow countrymen, this much I owe to myself."
The Budget-Mr. Dorion

As a result of this just, bold and courageous demand of Louis Hippolyte Lafontaine, in 1842, two years later, that is in 1844, the Canadian government requested an amendment to the Union Act to allow its citizens to express themselves in the French language in this parliament.
For this reason, I claim that it is absolutely true, in this circumstance as in all others, that the language and privileges of French Canadians have been recognized, mostly, if not entirely as a result of the efforts of our forefathers.
Reverting now to the matter under discussion, the budget, I consider it to be neither a literary work nor a problem in higher mathematics to be discussed by scientists or financial experts. It must be remembered that it is submitted to the people of the country. This is why I shall endeavour to express the views of the average taxpayer whose yearly income does not exceed a few thousand dollars and who belongs to the group making up at least 90 per cent of the total population of Canada. He, and he alone, the average taxpayer, should be the object of our thoughts, for what good are a few score millionaires when 90 per cent of our people are destitute?
For an appraisal of the policy we mean to adopt, we must therefore turn to the average taxpayer who cannot count on accumulating wealth, even if he wanted to, for it is known that a fervent aspiration of mankind is to set aside a certain amount of savings for the peace and comfort of old age. But no one will deny that, because he is burdened with the evergrowing responsibilities brought on by the high cost of living, the average taxpayer is now denied this legitimate ambition.
All the average taxpayer can now hope for, all he can demand, is to live comfortably, to marry and be in a position to allow his wife and children to have a comfortable life, free them from hardship and too much denial. He is the one therefore, who has first claim on the assistance of the government.
I have no fear for the rich and the mighty for experience has shown that, even in the worst depressions, they manage to get by and have the means to do so. See what is happening in the war-torn countries of Europe, in the grip of famine and of the black market. We all realize that the poor are still those who suffer and die. The moneyed classes manage very well.
I admit that low wage earners are somewhat relieved of income tax by the budget proposals, but these reductions are insufficient anil do not live up to the average taxpayers' expectations. Exemptions should have been fixed at $1,000 for single persons and $2,500 for

married persons. Other considerations than income tax must be taken into account. No one can deny that practically all taxes eventually press upon the consumers and the mass of the people.
In order to provide his family with food, clothing and living quarters, the ordinary tax-pare pays so much more for these necessities of life as the higher taxes levied on the merchant, the manufacturer or the landlord raise the price of goods and the rent of buildings.
That is why the average taxpayer is directly concerned not only with the part of his revenue collected by the government but with the total taxes making up the national revenue. What stands out in the budget is the enormous debt of the country, a debt which is constantly increasing and may never stop increasing, to a point that we must pay nearly $500 millions in interest, a burden which will fall upon the taxpayer. Our enormous debt has resulted from the extravagant expenditures of the last few years when the government led us to think that our war effort was to be reflected by the amount of our expenditures, whether they be justified or not.
It is not my intention to discuss again the question of our participation in the war; this is neither the right moment nor the right occasion. However, now that the war is over, we have the right to ask ourselves what have been the results of the sacrifices that we imposed upon ourselves during the past six years, and we also have the right to examine the consequences of the policy followed by this government throughout those years. We were told that we were fighting to save civilization. Will anyone contend that civilization, which we sought to defend, is not at the present time in as great, if not greater, danger than in 1939? Will anyone contend that the sacrifices and hardships which we have endured in the last few years have brought us that peace and tranquility which we were looking forward to? Is it not true that the world situation is to-day just as insecure as it was prior to the war? This is the thought which is in the mind of the taxpayer when he is required to pay heavy taxes in order to meet the enormous war debt. If at least he could think that the sacrifices which he has made and which he is still being asked to make were of some use. On the contrary, he is being made the target for an ever increasing amount of pernicious propaganda. He feels surrounded, almost smothered, by communistic propaganda whose object is to provoke here as elsewhere internal difficulties which will weaken nations and make them an easy prey for the monster which threatens the world at present.

The Budget-Mr. Dorion
May I recall an incident which took place in Quebec about three weeks ago. We were having the visit of a Belgian officer who had been a prisoner in the notorious and hellish Dachau concentration camp, from which only about ten per cent of the inmates came out alive. That Belgian officer came to this country to raise funds on behalf of the Belgian war orphans. After relating the hardships which he had to endure in the Dachau camp, he spoke of the communistic propaganda being carried out at the present time in his own country as well as in France, and of the means used to spread this subversive doctrine in those two countries. In conclusion he could not help exclaiming: "As you know, there were two monsters in Europe. We have destroyed one and we are now wondering if we have destroyed the worse one."
We have abundant evidence of this pernicious propaganda here in Canada. I only have to refer to the report of the Kellock-Taschereau investigation which was tabled yesterday in this house. May I refer to an item which appeared in Le Droit of Ottawa, on the Uth instant.
It is a dispatch from Regina, Saskatchewan, which reads as follows:
His Excellency Archbishop P. J. Monahan, ol Regina, has urged the delegates to the convention of the Saskatchewan French-Canadian Association, as well .as the delegates of the French Canadian School Trustees Association and those of the Catholic School Trustees Association, meeting jointly, in the basement of Holy Rosary cathedral, at Regina, ito oppose with the utmost energy the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation government's policy, which consists in appointing men who are publicly recognized as communists to high positions in the field of teaching and education in Saskatchewan.
"One of the greatest dangers which threaten democracy and all minorities, said His Excellency, is communism. To-day the greatest enemy of society, of religion and of Canada, he added, is communism. It is my duty, the archbishop continued, and it is your duty, as school trustees, to direct open protests to the prime minister and the other ministers of the Saskatchewan government, against the appointment of men -who are not acceptable to us and whose philosophy is a danger to adult education in this province.
Now, at this time when we feel much concern, as we might as well admit, we must nevertheless note that during the war, notwithstanding the sufferings, and the hardships that necessarily accompany this scourge of mankind, some people have succeeded, in this country, in accumulating wealth for more than $12,000,000,000, and we must now pay them a tribute of many millions a year in the form of interests, in recognition of the ability they showed, when, at a time when our soldiers were being killed, those people were 63260-222
accumulating dominion bonds. Mr. Speaker, no one had the right to make money out of the war.
To-day, in order to give some relief to the taxpayers, to do them the most elementary justice, the government should have the courage to restore the balance in demanding the return to the common fund, that is to the state, of at least part of the wealth that was accumulated during the war. Instead of that, new sources of income are sought and, as the taxation field is almost totally covered already, organizations such as cooperative associations, which should always have remained exempted, are brought under the fiscal measures.
I do not intend to delve deeply into the matter of taxation of cooperatives as proposed, for we shall have another opportunity of dealing with this question when the budget resolutions are submitted to us.
I shall be content to state that, to my mind, the principle of taxing these associations is opposed to the proper management of public affairs.
Indeed, it is generally admitted, to-day more than ever, that one of the foremost duties of any government, is to prevent, by all means at their disposal, that our people be led into reactionary movements.
I submit that the best way to ensure our population against the dangers of supporting subversive doctrines, is to give them the means and opportunity of acquiring a measure of wealth and becoming landowners.
Since it is difficult if not entirely impossible to conceive of all citizens individually acquiring property, we may, as an alternative, encourage them to joint ownership; such is the function of cooperative societies.
To my mind, therefore, the fact that cooperatives are organized and carry on remains one of the strongest ramparts for society in general against the increasingly dangerous tide of communistic ideologies.
The budget, however, ignores this principle; that is why, among several other reasons, I cannot approve the financial scheme as it was brought before us.
In support of this contention, I take the liberty of setting forth a piece of evidence which I consider noteworthy. About two weeks ago, while listening to a newscast, I heard that the new French minister of food, passing through Washington, was on his way back home. Asked how he intended to deal with the crisis which is rife in France, as it is all over Europe, the French minister of food, Mr. Yves Farge, stated that he had definitely resolved to fight the black market relentlessly

The Budget-Mr. Dorion

and that the expansion of cooperative societies in his country would provide the best means of putting teeth into his campaign.
It may be claimed that some cooperatives have, to a greater or lesser degree, become joint stock companies; that may be so, in certain cases, but we should have differentiated among the various types of cooperatives. I know, for instance, that in my riding, only two varieties are represented; they are the farmers' and fishermen's co-operatives. I am also convinced that these have never pocketed any real profits;, if they set aside reserve funds, their savings will be applied to the purchase of required farm machinery or fishing tackle which they lack and will use on a joint basis. This is also true of fishermen's co-operatives which also happen to put aside small savings, but no one could call it a reserve fund since the few hundred dollars which they save and which will be used to buy the necessary fishing gear. That is why I say that in taxing those reserves we are not taxing capital but the savings of the co-operator. That is how I happen to know that this plan is causing justified resentment in the province of Quebec, and besides it is not the sole cause of discontent.
When for instance we realize how federal affairs are being managed and consider the status of French Canadians in the civil service, we can easily see that our people very often have good cause to complain of the way they are treated. Thus statistics will show that in 1918, before the creation of the Civil Service Commission under the federal administration, the proportion of French Canadian civil servants amounted to 21-58 per cent while in 1946 the proportion was down to 12-25 per cent. What is worse, with respect to salaries of $6,000 or more a year ,the proportion of French Canadians fell from 25 per cent in 1918 to 9-52 per cent in 1946. According to a return which was tabled in the house at my request, out of 37 employees holding a rank comparable to that of deputy minister-indeed there is not a single full-fledged French Canadian deputy minister-5 only are French-Canadians.
Among the deputy ministers and those holding a rank comparable to that of deputy minister, one gets $15,000, four $12,000, fourteen $10,000, seven $9,000 and eleven $8,000 or less. Of course the five French Canadians who appear on that list fall in the last class, those receiving $8,000 or less.
The Prime Minister has tabled to-day the report of the royal commission investigating civil service conditions. Although I did not

have time to read the whole report, I glanced through- the summary of the recommendations appearing in the first part of the report. I have failed to find any remedy to this situation which was forcefully outlined to that commission by the chamber of commerce of the district of Montreal. In this connection I wish to endorse the conclusions reached in a splendid report prepared by the latter, which was submitted to the commission in April, 1946.
It is not only the civil service, Mr. Speaker, that French Canadians are complaining about. For instance, in Quebec, in the district and city of Quebec, there are many unemployed for whom jobs will have to be found shortly. At Quebec there are thousands of unemployed who, at the present time are drawing unemployment benefits, but before long they will be without means of providing a living for their family. On the other hand, in Quebec, there are large plants, namely that of St. Malo, for instance, for which the country spent millions of dollars, that are now absolutely idle; at the same time we are receiving letters from farmers in our constituencies requesting our help in securing farm implements which they badly need, and contractors complain that they are unable to obtain building materials.
What is lacking then? The plants are owned by the dominion government and it would be easy for them to take the necessary steps in order to put them into operation and manufacture farm implements or building materials which are so urgently needed, and at the same time provide work for the unemployed.
I am no socialist, far from it. I have said before and I repeat that I am in favour of private enterprise, but when it has failed, it seems to me that it is up to government authorities to organize an industry, the need of which is admitted by everyone.
Another complaint against the federal government concerns the inactivity of Quebec harbour. It is generally recognized that since the control of national harbours has been centralized, the Quebec harbour is noted for its idleness by river travellers. In days gone by, as everyone knows, the harbour at Quebec was always doing big business and I well remember the time when the Quebec harbour commission employed many Quebec workers. If the Quebec harbour were to regain its former animation, I am convinced that the labour problem could be very easily solved in the city itself as well as in the whole district.

The Budget-Mr. LaCroix
At present, the Quebec harbour is altogether idle. I am quoting statistics for the year 1943, published in the 1945 Canada Year Book which are, I believe, the latest available. On page 696, I find that in that year, 177 ships entered the Quebec harbour while 720 docked at Halifax, 593 at St. John's, 123 at Trois-Rivieres, that is, almost as many as at Quebec, and so on. This is conclusive evidence that as long as the harbour administration is controlled by this central commission in Ottawa, the Quebec harbour will remain idle and Quebec workers unemployed.
The government might undertake quite a few work programmes in my riding, for the constituency of Charlevoix-Saguenay is known as the largest in the dominion. It extends on the north shore of the St. Lawrence river for 900 miles, from Quebec city to Blanc-Sablon in the strait of Belle-Isle. Of all necessity, means of communication should be provided to allow people in that vast district to get in touch with the outside. What we need most there is wharves and protective- works, and it is obvious that we would have to do twenty times more than is being done at present. [DOT] When our people consider the gifts of millions of dollars made to foreign countries-indeed I have always considered the loan which was made as a gift-while at home our people, our fishermen and our farmers, are awaiting various projects and the building of means of communication which would enable them to sell their products, I say that those people have reason to be dissatisfied and to protest against this state of affairs.
I trust therefore that the situation will be remedied so that these people may get the means of communication which are so urgently required.
There is another point to which I would only refer in passing, the offer to the various provinces contained in the budget speech. Obviously everyone regrets the failure of the dominion-provincial conference; everyone hopes that it will be resumed and that a fair agreement will be reached in the best interests of the country and of the provinces. But in this connection it must be remembered that if we may hold views on the position taken by the dominion government and that taken by the provinces, the people of Canada are entitled to their own opinions regarding dominion-provincial relations. I wish to recall to the government that a by-election was held recently in the constituency of Compton and that the people there were called upon to approve the position taken by the dominion government and that taken by the Prime Minister of Quebec. We all know the result.

The voters of that constituency, which includes both French and English speaking citizens, endorsed by an overwhelming majority the attitude of the Prime Minister of Quebec.

dends will not be subjected to income tax. If I am wrong, I ask him to correct me when he makes his speech to close the debate. Allow me to point out to you, Mr. Speaker, that our co-operative associations are very important, since they are such that they do away with the middleman and establish direct relations between the farmer and the consumer.
The cooperative associations are non-profit organizations, making it possible for the farmers to buy collectively what they need. At home, in the old province of Quebec, they are the only means of fighting trusts, chain stores and large business enterprises.
I believe that the farmer cooperative associations now existing constitute the surest way of ensuring economic independence to our population. I wish to protest strongly against taxation of reserves which are so essential to the maintenance of the value of the equipment of our cooperative associations and also against taxation of patronage dividends either actually paid out or credited to the membership.
We have already met the Right Hon.. Minister of Finance on several occasions in this connection and I dare hope he will take into consideration the views of hon. members of both sides of the House who seem unanimous on this matter. Any other course of action would constitute an encouragement to the trusts and would lead our people into the most thorough socialism, so earnestly desired by the C.C.F. party.
Mr. Speaker, may I therefore make a final appeal in this connection to the Right Hon. Minister of Finance? I must also register a strong protest against the fact that the small taxpayer was not granted relief by increased exemptions on small incomes.
May I ask the Right Hon. Minister of Finance that, when those resolutions are submitted to us, he consider granting full tax exemption to all who earn less than S3,000 a year.
I appreciate what difficulties may stand in the way of tax exemptions in view of the many billion-dollar gifts to Great Britain and of certain interest-free loans of other billions. I hope that common sense will finally come into its own and that due regard will be had for the fact that we should first look after our own welfare.
It seems ridiculous to me how Conservative, C.C.F. and Social Credit members, having endorsed billion-dollar gifts to Great Britain and interest-free loans of other billions, should now

complain in this house that taxes are too high. They are the ones who, in constantly outbidding the financial policy of the government, drove us into the present chaos.

It had been my intention to devote the forty minutes of my talk on the budget to War Assets Corporation and its workings throughout the past two or three years because, in my opinion, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) has missed a great bet. I believe we could wipe out the entire estimated deficit of this year's budget by a proper distribution and proper use of the assets held by Canada at the close of the war and as a result of the sudden cessation of hostilities.
The story has been pretty well told in one of Canada's magazines. There is, for example, the story of an employee of Research Enterprises who tried to buy some of this material after it had been reduced to junk and was told that he could not do so because he was an employee of the concern. A couple of years later he went back to the same man in the same position and asked whether he could buy the same material at a price twice as much as was charged for junk, and he was informed that he could not do so because he was not an employee. There is the story of a typical case of a war veteran and his efforts to obtain machine tools to reestablish himself in his industry. We have the story of War Assets and their 15,000 cars and trucks resold to dealers and manufacturers. There is the example of 48 four-wheel drive trucks which cost the government 811,350, which were sold back to the assemblers or the manufacturers at about 84,801 each and were resold to priority claimers at from $6,800 to $7,200 each. There is the story of an enterprising aeroplane dealer from New York, Charles Babb and Company, who bought 185 Finch aircraft from the Canadian government at a price of $302 each when a private individual had a hard job getting anything. There is a report on how not to buy an aeroplane. I believe another article is going to appear, but at this time I would congratulate the Maclean Publishing Company on the work they are doing in exposing what, in my opinion, is one of the black pages of Canada's war record, and that is War Assets Corporation. I know my own efforts over a couple of years are a story of complete frustration; for I have tried in vain to get questions answered, even on the order paper, and in the committee I have tried to get information, but one is

speechtext:
I had just about finished anyway. I did not think the rule preventing the member from saying anything was to be extended to the budget. I have been trying to get information about War Assets, but I did not think the rule was going to be applied to this extent. I could have spent forty minutes on that particular story which would have brought us up to date on where the present government stands. It would have added to their record of 1944 when the Liberal

administration, by order in council, handed over to the Imperial Oil, a subsidiary of the Standard Oil Company, the tremendous oil resources of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. I could have spent forty minutes of my time on the budget in discussing the matter of farmers' income tax, if it is not before a committee. I could have discussed with the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) the fact that, although the budget allows a farmer to average his income over a three-year period, it has not yet tackled the problem of the farm income tax, because basically it differs in many ways from the ordinary business proposition. The ordinary business man carries on his work in his little business. He leaves his home and goes to his business place. He hires people to do his work and he is permitted, as deductible from his profits, the income that is paid as wages to those who assist him in earning that income. In the case of the farmer, his wife and children work on the farm, but there is n<j allowance for wages that might be paid because no wages are paid. The largest army of unpaid workers in Canada are the workers on the farms. To face up to this problem in all fairness, the minister should. grant exemption of at least $3,000 for the woman and the family who work on the farm. That would permit the farmer to bring the earnings of the family into equity and make it possible for him to carry on. Something has to be done in that regard to bring back into the minds of the Canadian people the proper place that agriculture has in our economy, to encourage the people to come back into production, to entice the young people particularly to go and work on farms. To-day they do not want to come back to the farms, and something is needed to rectify that situation.
But when the minister completed the reading of that part of his budget dealing with the taxation of cooperatives I recognized at once an attack on the cooperative way of life. After reading the budget through a couple of times,
I came to the conclusion that this resolution is designed to go deeper at the roots of the cooperative way of life than would possibly be imagined on first reading. I should like to warn the government that when it sets out to cripple the cooperative movement in Canada and destroy the very basis of the principles of cooperation it is aligning itself against the masses of the people, and putting itself by the side of those who stand in special privileged positions, monopolistic industry, the grain exchange, and so on. Apparently the campaign of the taxpayers' association which must have cost hundreds of thousands of dollars has worked so far as the government is concerned. The minister has started out on a road which

The Budget-Mr. Castleden
will be filled with thorns. He is on a road which will be filled with opposition. This group to which I belong, the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, which believes basically in the cooperative way of life, are going to fight with everything they have.
When the budget speech informed us that section 4 (p) of the Income War Tax Act would be repealed we knew that the lid was off. Here is the government, returned by the people in 1945, cutting at the very roots of the cooperative movement, which plays a valuable part in the economic life of all countries. Big business is showing its hand to-day. It is a mailed fist, and it is out to render the cooperative movement in Canada useless as a weapon by which the small man, the person in the lower income group, can protect himself against those who would establish a complete monopoly, either in services or in commodities, and compel the rank and file of the people to pay their price because they can maintain it in scarcity. I charge this government with aiding and abetting that movement. I should like to refer to pages 29 and 30 of the report of the royal commission on cooperatives, where they outline the public interest of cooperatives in the life of any country. The report says:
The representatives of cooperative associations advanced two main grounds upon which they sought to be freed from tax. They urged, in the first place, that their associations performed certain public services for people in receipt of low incomes which ordinary companies did not attempt, or at least not to the same extent . . . Secondly, it was alleged that they were not profit-making institutions by intention or practice; that their object was to perform services for their members at cost, giving rise to the argument that, in fact, they did not derive profits from their members.
The social and economic advantages to the people of Canada are not small. Again on page 30 they say:
The commission is in no doubt that the cooperative associations can and do perform services which are valuable not only to their members but redound to the advantage of the community in general. . . In particular, the cooperative form of organization, especially in rural areas, affords an opportunity to individual members of outstanding capacity to obtain an experience in management, administration and leadership which, in the ordinary course of events, they could not obtain in any other way.
Further they say:
Some representatives of the cooperative associations argued, and it was repeated on many occasions, that the methods of cooperation resting. as they say, upon the self help motif, appealed to and developed a higher set of principles than the individual and purely selfish pursuit of gain.
Cooperation is an essential part of democracy. In Scotland and England, allied with the labour movement the great Scottish and British cooperatives ha've fought a battle for a hundred years to maintain their existence. Apparently the battle is to be joined here too. In Sweden, in the United States, in Canada, in China, in Denmark and for a while in Germany, progress in almost every country has been in direct proportion to the extent the people have the ability to democratically organize and completely work their cooperative organizations. Is it not a significant fact that when fascism comes in, the ultimate of monopoly enterprise, the first things that have to go in any country are the cooperative movement and the labour movement. Hitler did it in Germany.

I am sure the people of Saskatchewan will appreciate that. The Minister of Finance has used the report of this royal commission as a screen from behind which he can attack the cooperatives. Yet he claims that in general he has followed their recommendations. Where the commission does not recommend that the government go farther, however, the minister goes the rest of the way himself. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bentley) and the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) have outlined the democratic basis of this great people's movement. They have told the story of the early fight of the grain growers in the west to organize their cooperative movement. Cooperatives are not profit-making organizations. Their purpose is to provide the people who
The Budget-Mr. Castleden

patronize them, whether producers or consumers, either with commodities at a proper cost, or with services, which services have not been available to them in the past unless they paid exorbitant prices for them. Cooperatives have grown up as the only means whereby the rank and file, the common people, can protect themselves against the vagaries and vicissitudes imposed upon them by those who get control by monopolies.
There are three points with which I want to deal briefly. The first is the legislation passed by the Liberal government in 1930, which this government claims was ambiguous and perhaps doubtful. I am going to point out that in the present legislation the government is striking at the very basis of cooperative principles, and that if this taxation goes through on the basis at present advocated it may not kill but certainly will cripple the cooperative movement and prevent it from growing. I claim further that this government has extremely weak grounds for going after the cooperatives and taxing them retroactively. Tor that purpose I will refer to the stand of the Liberal party as set out in Hansard for May 24, 1930, when the then Minister of Finance, Hon. C. A. Dunning, brought in the legislation. Here is his budget resolution as it appears at page 2505 of Hansard for 1930:
2. That the income of cooperative companies and associations be exempt from income tax.
Then at page 2507 I find this discussion:
...Mr.. Hanson; Does this arise out of the litigation in relation to the wheat pool?
Mr. Dunning: No.
Mr. Hanson: There was litigation, was there not, between the department and the wheat pool over the question of payment of income tax?
Mr. Dunning: Yes.
Mr. Hanson: What was the decision?
Mr. Dunning: It was decided against the department by the Supreme Court of Canada.
Mr. Hanson: That is exactly what I thought was the case. Is the litigation ended?
Mr. Dunning: The litigation is ended.
., Mr, Hanson: If that be so, and you have ihe decision of the highest court of appeal in this country, why the necessity of this legislation?
An hon. Member:	There are other cooperatives.
Mr. Hanson: I know, but the principle is there established.
Mr. Dunning: Oh, no; it was a question of contract, and the interpretation of a contract. It did not bear specific relationship to the nature of the organization.
And listen to this, by Mr. Dunning:
The intention here is to exempt bona fide cooperative associations and companies from income tax. I can better discuss the details when the bill is presented, and hon. members will have the proposed sections before them. It 
is difficult to make a statement when the bill is not before the house, but I may say that a bona fide cooperative organization shall be exempt entirely from the provisions of the Income War Tax Act. I may read what is contained in the bill, although hon. members will understand that the bill cannot be introduced until the resolution has been adopted by the house.
Then he proceeded to read section 4 of the act, which was tc be amended by adding thereto the following paragraph, and here is paragraph (p):
(p) The income of farmers', dairymen's, live-stockmen's, fruit growers', poultrymen's, fishermen's and other like cooperative companies and associations whether with or without share capita] organized and operated on a cooperative basis, which organizations-
(a)	market the products of the members or shareholders of such cooperative organizations under an obligation to pay to them the proceeds from the sales on the basis of quantity and quality less necessary expenses and reserves;
(b)	purchase supplies and equipment for the use of such members under an obligation to turn such supplies and equipment over to them at cost, plus necessary expenses and reserves.
Such companies and associations may market the produce of, or purchase supplies and equipment for non-members of the company or association provided the value thereof does not exceed 20 per centum of the value of produce, supplies or equipment marketed or purchased for the members or shareholders.
Then followed this statement by Mr. Dunning, and I should like to emphasize it:
That means that any cooperative organization falling within the groups there mentioned or other like groups may do business for its own shareholders provided that the arrangement of the business is to return all proceeds less the necessary reserves and expenses to those who contribute the commodities or, in the second place, in the case of the purchasing association, to those who purchase the goods.
I read this to show the house that what was intended by the legislation was clear beyond doubt. That was the Liberal party in 1930. What has been brought down to-day is a complete reversal of that. At the time the resolution was brought in, there was no question of doubt as to what it was for. There was no question in the house, and no question in the mind of the minister. Still we now have a doubt raised. The matter is not even brought to the courts.
The minister bases his argument upon some pretence that this is ambiguous, and that the intention was not clear. Then we have the commission being set up.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like a great many hon. members who have already spoken, I may say that I did not intend to enter into this debate, but always something arises to incite one to say a few words on an important matter like the bduget. I rise particularly for two reasons, and I can express them in a very short time.
First of all, I wish to associate myself with the hon. gentlemen who have given the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) such deserved compliments, and I wish to endorse the statements of some hon. members who designated the minister as the best finance minister this dominion has had since the days of confederation. That is one reason why I attempt to say a few words in this debate. Another is to make a few remarks as to what I personally think of this budget.
It is my opinion that it is a matter-of-fact presentation of our financial position. I do not believe that this budget could be expected to be very bright and cheery on account of the awful experience to which the treasury has been subjected. It was encouraging at least to see that the deficit was reduced so substantially from last year, but those who hoped for larger tax reductions were somewhat disappointed. To me it appears that the budget is a forceful reminder to the Canadian people that we have emerged from the most devastating war in history, and while we have achieved victory on the battlefield, we must continue to fight with sacrifice and determination against other dangers which threaten us. Our assumption of obligations in the remaking of the world and our obligations to those who fought for us are important factors in the budget. War was costly and produced only destruction; rehabilitation is costly but 
will produce good citizens of our land, and in some measure, repay the debt we owe to those who left home and loved ones to endure hardships and face death to protect our way of life.
The finance minister is making another effort to bring about a dominion-provincial conference. If we are ever going to get anywhere, we must face up to our national problems as Canadians, not as citizens of the maritimes, Quebec, Ontario or the west. Therefore we must earnestly hope that these last proposals will result in some amicable agreement between the provinces and the federal government.
The budget contains a clause allowing farmers and fishermen to pay taxes on a three-year average rather than on a single year's operations. It was unfair that a farmer or fisherman, so dependent on nature for success should be taxed on, say a $5,000 income this year if last year he actually lost $3,000. The fairness of this proposal, which has been long discussed here, will, I think, receive general applause.
While the step-up in exemption figures was not as great as was hoped for, it should be kept in mind that our figure here is higher than in the United States, Britain or New Zealand. The exemption limits under the present tax are $660 for single persons and, in effect, $1,200 for married persons. As a major part of the present revision, it is proposed that the exemptions be raised to $750 for single persons, and $1,500 for married persons without dependents. This measure, taken in conjunction with the proposal regarding allowances for dependents, will remove entirely from the income tax roll between 550,000 and 600,000 taxpayers, or about one-quarter of the present number. The proposed exemptions will be in the form of deductions from income in the manner of the pre-war exemptions, and the $1,500 deduction will replace the combined income deduction of $660 and the tax credit of $150 granted to married men under the present law.
Consideration was given by the finance minister to suggestions made by persons who may not be familiar with all the facts, that the exemption limits be raised to $1,000 for single persons and $2,000 for married persons, and even that the exemptions be $1,200 and $2,400 respectively. After careful examination of these and other suggestions, the minister came to the conclusion that exemptions of $750 and $1,500 respectively are as high as can reasonably be proposed under present circumstances.

Privilege-Mr. Fraser
In the first place, we must still raise very large amounts of revenue. Even if no tax reductions were made, our revenues will fall considerably short of our expenditures and far short of our total financial requirements for the current year. Moreover, there is already a great excess of purchasing power and we must not add unnecessarily to it. In addition to these immediate considerations, we must bear in mind that the government and parliament face a post-war period in which events are likely to move swiftly, and in respect of which we have accepted a large measure of responsibility for maintaining high employment. Under these circumstances we cannot afford- to reduce our revenues too drastically.
Second, we are all, I believe, agreed that the income tax is the fairest and best tax on which to rely for the bulk of our revenue. More than any other tax, it takes ability to pay properly. into account. We must, I consider, rely upon it as heavily as we can, subject to the limits imposed by its effects on incentive and efficiency. This applies as well in the lower backets a' in the higher. We cannot secure proper equity and fair treatment if exemptions from income tax are so high as to exclude most of those receiving incomes. It is just as important to be fair in the distribution of taxation between persons earning $1,500 and $2,400 a year respectively, as it is to be fair in the distribution of taxation between these persons and those earning $5,000 or $10,000 a year. I have said that we cannot afford to reduce our revenues beyond reasonable figures. In these circumstances, if we raised unreasonably the exemptions for the income tax, or lowered the rates of income tax too drastically, we would only make it necessary to impose other less equitable, even regressive, forms of taxes.
Comparison of our proposed exemptions with those of other countries indicates clearly, I believe, that the figures now proposed are as high as Canada can reasonably go. The suggested exemption of $750 for the single person compares with one of $700 in Australia and New Zealand, of $500 in the United States, and of $490 in Britain. Similarly, the proposed exemption of $1,500 for a married person compares with $1,077 in New Zealand, $1,000 in the United States, $931 in Australia and $800 in Britain. In addition, Britain, Australia and New Zealand have substantial social security taxes which apply at much lower levels than the exemptions I have given for income tax alone.
